newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler May U.S. vehicle sales drop 16.6 percent.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler May U.S. vehicle sales drop 16.6 percent.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said Monday sales fell 16.6 percent in May from a record month in 1996 due to weaker consumer demand and an engine plant strike that curtailed truck and Jeep production.
The nation's third-largest automaker said sales for the month totalled 204,654 cars and trucks, compared with 245,289 in May 1996, its all-time record sales month.
Chrysler's passenger car sales fell 17.9 percent from a year ago to 72,944 units, while truck sales, normally a source of strength for Chrysler, were off 15.5 percent to 131,710 units.

"Even allowing for the strike and the tough comparison with last year, these are weak numbers," said Burnham Securities analyst David Healy. "It's partly a payback from the unsustainably high sales rate in the first three months of the year."

U.S. light vehicle sales in May were expected to reach a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 14.9 million units, the second month in a row that sales have fallen significantly below the first-quarter rate of about 15.6 million units.

Analysts said part of the slowdown came from a drop in used-car prices, which reduces trade-in values and makes lease payments more expensive. Fierce competition and strong incentives in the first quarter also pulled some spring sales forward, said CS First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas.

"The spring market isn't as strong as we thought it would be, but the summer market seems to be coming back," said Steve Torok, Chrysler's executive director of sales and marketing, adding consumers remain confident and interest rates stable.
"We think our core product lines -- minivans, trucks, sport utilities -- all look very healthy right now," he said.
Chrysler halted production of four truck models during a month-long strike at its Mound Road Engine Plant in Detroit, which formally ended May 9.

The strike cut off supplies of the automaker's V-8 and V-6 truck engines and reduced sales of the Dodge Ram pickup truck, the Dakota pickup, the Ram van and the Jeep Grand Cherokee by about 15 percent, Torok said.
Ram pickup sales fell 36 percent from a year earlier to 23,852 units, which also was down 22 percent from April 1997.
May Grand Cherokee fell 16 percent from a year ago and Ram van sales dropped 69 percent. Dodge Dakota pickup sales rose 18 percent from a year earlier but were down 15 percent from April.
Sales of other vehicles not affected by the strike also fell. Sales of its redesigned Cherokee fell 7 percent from year-ago levels, and minivan sales were down 6 percent.

All Chrysler's passenger car models showed declines except for the Dodge Stratus, which registered an 8 percent increase over year-ago levels. Stratus sales in May included significant deliveries to rental fleets, a spokesman said.
Analysts expect General Motors Corp. also to report a May sales decline Tuesday, and Ford Motor Co. to report lower sales Wednesday.
Among other automakers Subaru, a unit of Fuji Heavy Industries Ltd., said May sales rose 0.2 percent to 9,630 units, with sales of imported cars up 4.4 percent and U.S.-built cars down 1.1 percent.
Sweden's AB Volvo said its import car sales for the month rose 4.4 percent to 8,709 units.
